title: The 20 Habits That Stop a Leader
author: The Business Leader Daily
summary: Based on Marshall Goldsmith's book What Got You Here Won't Get You There, this article argues that what holds back accomplished leaders is not a lack of competence but a set of behavioral habits that everyone around them can see and they cannot. Goldsmith found that most accomplished people succeed not because of their worst habits but in spite of them, and half the leaders he worked with didn't need additional competencies — they needed to quit one behavior. His list of twenty habits includes winning too much, adding too much value, passing judgment, starting with 'no but however,' withholding information, claiming unearned credit, and refusing to express regret. The remedy Goldsmith prescribes is deceptively simple: pick one behavior, ask colleagues for one or two suggestions for the future rather than relitigating the past, say thank you without defending or justifying, and actually work on it.
points: What holds back accomplished leaders is rarely competence — by the time someone reaches a senior seat, almost everyone is capable; the separator is behavioral habits that others see clearly and the leader cannot.
Goldsmith's key insight is to teach leaders to stop rather than add: half the leaders he met didn't need additional competencies, they needed to quit one behavior that was costing them the room.

The twenty habits include winning too much, adding too much value to every idea, starting sentences with 'No/But/However,' speaking when angry, withholding information, and an excessive need to be 'me.'

Awareness of these habits is necessary but nowhere near sufficient — most people who acknowledge the need to change never act, so Goldsmith built a process specifically designed to defeat that failure.

The remedy: pick one behavior, ask colleagues for suggestions about the future (not the past), say thank you without defending or justifying, and actually work on it — the discomfort is the doorway to the next level.
quotes: What if some of the things you are most proud of are now the things holding you back?
By the time you reach a senior seat, almost everyone around you is capable. The thing separating good from great at that altitude is not another technical skill. It is behavior.
most accomplished people often succeed not because of their worst habits but in spite of them.
Half the leaders Goldsmith met didn’t need any additional competencies. They needed to quit one behavior that was costing them the room.

Winning too much. The need to win at all costs and in all situations, when it matters, when it doesn’t, and when it’s beside the point. Goldsmith calls it the most common behavioral problem in successful people.

Adding too much value. The overwhelming urge to improve every idea someone brings you by tacking on your two cents. You may slightly raise the idea’s quality, but you sharply lower the other person’s commitment to it.

Instead of asking people to relitigate what you did wrong, which invites defensiveness on your side and discomfort on theirs, you ask a different question. Pick one behavior you want to improve, go to the people around you, and ask for one or two suggestions for the future.
